newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: UNIDO regrets Britain's plan to quit agency.
newsitem.headline: UNIDO regrets Britain's plan to quit agency.

text.p: The head of the United Nations development body expressed shock on Tuesday at Britain's planned withdrawal and said if Germany followed suit the organisation could face big problems.
Britain said in a letter to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Monday that it intended to quit the U.N. Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) by the end of 1997.

"I was shocked by the announcement made by the British government...regarding the decision of the U.K. to leave UNIDO starting in 1998," UNIDO director-general Mauricio de Maria y Campos told a news conference.
The Vienna-based organisation promotes industrialisation in the developing world. It has seen interest wane as budget-conscious governments look to cut costs.
The UNIDO head criticised the decision, which he said did not take account of the agency's sweeping reforms since 1993.
"I think it's quite unfair this trend that is taking place to chastise UNIDO and to put it at ransom to what happens on the level of U.N. reform," Maria y Campos of Mexico said.
German Development Minister Carl-Dieter Spranger said last month that 1997 budget cuts had forced him to opt for withdrawal from UNIDO, the first time Bonn would have quit any U.N. agency.

German newspapers reported on Tuesday Bonn would suspend the plan to withdraw from the agency, fearing such a move could damage its chances of becoming a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council.
Maria y Campos said he would be very concerned if both Germany and Britain, who together contribute 20 percent of UNIDO's annual $79 million budget, left the organisation.
"It would not be very easy (to cope) if Germany left, without major cuts to UNIDO programmes," he said.
The German daily Handelsblatt said Germany was likely to stay in UNIDO for a year while it considered whether the body was reforming itself.
"I have had no official communication of this," Maria y Campos said. "I hope it is confirmed."

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said in his letter to Boutros-Ghali that London would decide at the end of 1997 whether it could rescind the decision if progress had been made on wider institutional reform.
The United States announced last year it was leaving the agency at the end of 1996, complaining of inefficiency. The pullout takes effect on December 31.
UNIDO has reduced its budget by a quarter, scrapped an entire tier of senior management and reduced its staff by 38 percent since 1993, it said.

Maria y Campos expressed the hope that the tide was turning back in UNIDO's favour. "It would seem that in the case of Germany a process of reflection has taken place since the first intention was mentioned by Minister Spranger," he noted.
